JOE DOWLING · REVIEWED DRAFT · 30 SEPTEMBER 2026

How easy is it to reduce an AI model’s refusal behaviour? Surprisingly easy.

A project to travel deep inside an open-weight LLM, discover how 'refusal' manifests itself, and perform mathematical brain surgery to reduce it in the model.

This project is yet another side-quest from my plan to build and train an LLM from scratch, however, after reading about 'abliteration' and doing some research, I decided that the associated learning would be worth the time investment. As a result, this article is focused on the theory but I have tried my best to keep it readable.

Inside a transformer model, every token is represented as a vector, basically a long ordered list of numbers. In the case of the model I used, this vector has 12,288 BF16 (16-bit) numbers, so each token is represented by a 24 KiB vector (24,576 bytes). Every token has its own 12,288-dimensional vector. For example, a 50-token prompt has 50 vectors, containing 50 × 12,288 numbers in total flowing through the layers. This per-token vector is called the token's residual stream, and as it flows through the model's layers, (88 of them in this case), the model reads the current set of 12,288 numbers, passes them through several weight matrices and adds the result back to the residual stream.

This journey allows the model to understand context, and the final values after all 88 layers are what the model uses to decide what to say next (the next token).

Diving Deeper into the 88 Layers - Attention & MLP

Each of the 88 layers is described here using seven main projection matrices across attention and a gated MLP; this simplifies away normalisation and other architecture details.

The attention block first uses three matrices — q_proj , k_proj , and v_proj — to turn each token's vector into three specialised vectors that can be thought of as a query “what am I looking for?” a key “what do I offer to the query?” and a value “what will I add if selected?” The model compares queries against keys across every token in the current sequence to decide which tokens should pay attention to which.

This is the step where the model can take a word like 'it' and can reach back and pull in information from the noun it refers to. The gathered result is then passed through a fourth matrix, o_proj , which produces the attention block's contribution to add back onto the residual stream.

The MLP block is where most of the raw computation happens. It first uses two matrices — up_proj and gate_proj — to expand the 12,288 numbers into a wider intermediate space whose size depends on the model configuration, applies a nonlinear function that lets the model represent more complex relationships, and then uses a third matrix, down_proj , to compress the result back down to 12,288 numbers, which it then adds back to the residual stream.

One key point for this project, of the 7 matrices named above, o_proj and down_proj are the only two matrices that write to the residual stream. Here I will call them output projections; they are not the same thing as individual attention heads.

The Search for Meaning, Behaviour and Refusal

The residual-stream activations are coordinates in a high-dimensional space; the weight matrices are learned transformations of those activations. We cannot assign definitions within the 12,288 numbers and simply read our way through the model to understand behaviour.

Meaning can be encoded in patterns across many activation coordinates at once. Some features can be represented approximately by directions in this space. A direction is itself represented by a vector; the analogy is an arrow, while an activation is a point. Both are expressed in the same coordinate system.

This direction is the phenomenon that we are interested in, it represents what the model has learned; both its representation of meaning and its learned behaviour. Behaviour is the important concept. A model learns behaviour in two ways; firstly, it learns patterns from the implicit human norms (politeness, formality, refusal etc) in the internet text used in training. Secondly, and more importantly, developers use alignment techniques (reinforcement learning from human feedback, supervised fine-tuning and 'constitutional AI', where written principles guide training feedback).

The trained behaviour we are interested in for this project is the model's refusal to respond to a range of nefarious, dangerous or unethical requests.

Given the huge scope of training, the massive number (12,288) of dimensions inside of the model, and thus the infinite number of possible directions, it would be normal to expect that the directions which trigger refusal are scattered across many different paths. However, a 2024 paper by Andy Arditi and colleagues found a direction that strongly mediated refusal in each of the 13 chat models they studied. This does not establish that all refusal in every model has one universal direction.

Source: Arditi et al. 2024 — refusal direction study

"Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions"

— Arditi et al, 2024

Source: Arditi et al. 2024 — refusal direction study

The research finding is that if a token's internal state is pushed toward that 'refusal' direction, the model is likely to refuse, even for harmless requests. Push a token away and refusals decrease. Removing that component substantially reduced refusal in the models and tests studied. This is evidence relevant to the broader linear representation hypothesis: some features are represented approximately by directions in activation space. It is not a guarantee about every behaviour or model.

Source: Arditi et al. 2024 — refusal direction study

Finding the refusal direction in the model - two clouds of dots

This is another abstract mental visualisation (realised with help from Gemini) but let’s stick with it as it will be useful later. The refusal direction does not come pre-labelled inside the model. It has to be calculated from evidence.

The method is called difference of means:

Create two sets of prompts, 400 harmful or refusal-triggering, and 400 similar but harmless ones. Run both sets through the model, but instead of reading the output, capture the internal state of the 12,288 directional vector at target layers for the last token of each prompt.

No weights are changed during this step. It is purely an observational pass to capture how the model's internal state differs when processing a harmful request versus a harmless one.

To capture this internal state we go into the model and record the 12,288 vector of the last token position from the residual stream at one of the 88 layers (eg 'layer 40'). The final prompt position is useful here because it has 'seen' the entire prompt thanks to attention processing in previous layers. The last token in the stream is closest to what the model is going to say next, so if the model is about to refuse, that position can carry a useful refusal signal. The strongest layer and token position need to be selected and validated for the model. To be more specific on the difference of means therefore:

Source: Arditi et al. 2024 — refusal direction study

Create two sets of prompts, 400 harmful or refusal-triggering, and 400 similar but harmless ones. Run each prompt forward through the model. At layer 40, capture the 12,288 number vector sitting at the final token position.

for each coordinate i = 1 ... 12,288:
    mean_harmful[i] = (h1[i] + h2[i] + ... + h400[i]) / 400
    mean_harmless[i] = (b1[i] + b2[i] + ... + b400[i]) / 400

# h and b denote activations from the two different prompt sets.

This gives us two centre-of-mass vectors and the refusal direction is just the difference between the two (coordinate by coordinate):

r_raw = mean_harmful − mean_harmless

The resulting 12,288 vector points from the 'this is harmless' state towards the 'I am going to refuse' state. The last step is to normalise the vector to unit length - dividing all 12,288 by the vector's overall length so that the whole vector has a length of 1 (Euclidean length). This keeps the direction of refusal while discarding the magnitude (we are interested in the direction of refusal, not the amount of refusal):

r̂ = r_raw / ‖r_raw‖, provided ‖r_raw‖ > 0

This is what I have attempted to visualise in the Gemini-generated schematic, rather than a plot of the measured data: two clouds of dots, green being the final token position of 400 harmless prompts, red being the final token position of 400 harmful prompts, all captured at layer 40 of the model, with the direction (r̂) as the arrow between them.

Removing Refusal - Performing Brain Surgery

As tokens pass through the model and trigger activations, we need to strip out refusal. This is done by an operation called vector projection. We use r̂ (our refusal direction) to measure how much refusal there is in a given activation (a) and subtract the component along that direction, leaving the orthogonal components unchanged. That geometric property does not guarantee that all other behaviours are preserved.

a_no_refusal = a − (r̂ · a) × r̂

where (r̂ · a) is the dot product resulting in a single scalar, ie

(r̂ · a) = (r̂1 × a1) + (r̂2 × a2) + (r̂3 × a3) + ... + (r̂12288 × a12288)

The dot product (r̂ · a) is critical here, it measures how much the two vectors point in the same direction, or, how much of the activation (a) sits along the refusal direction r̂. Only r̂ has been normalised here, so r̂ · a = ‖a‖ cos(θ): it is the signed projection length. It equals cosine similarity only if a is also a unit vector. A large positive number means that the activation is heavily aligned to the refusal direction. Near zero means little component along this particular direction, not proof that refusal is absent. To do a worked example using a 3 dimensional vector to remove high refusal;

r̂ = [2/3, 2/3, 1/3]  (exact unit vector)
a = [3, 1, 1]
Step 1 — calculate the dot product:
  r̂ · a = (2/3 × 3) + (2/3 × 1) + (1/3 × 1)
         = 2 + 2/3 + 1/3
         = 3
Step 2 — rebuild the component along r̂:
  3 × [2/3, 2/3, 1/3] = [2, 2, 1]
Step 3 — remove that component:
  a_no_refusal = [3, 1, 1] − [2, 2, 1] = [1, −1, 0]

So in this simple three-dimensional example, the activation changes from [3, 1, 1] to [1, −1, 0], which is orthogonal to r̂. This demonstrates the projection operation; it does not by itself prove that the first vector would cause a refusal, or that all other model behaviour is unchanged. Those are empirical questions.

To 'implement' the brain surgery, we adjust the model's weights by precisely the calculated amount (software optimisation tools can do this easily). Given that o_proj and down_proj are the only heads which write to the residual stream in each of the 88 layers, those two projections across 88 layers give 176 matrices. Other writes, such as the input embedding or biases where present, require separate consideration; this count alone is not a complete account of an implementation.

Source: Arditi et al. 2024 — refusal direction study

The result? These edited projections no longer add a component along the selected direction. In the experiment below, refusal became much less frequent. That is a striking result, but it does not mean the model has lost every possible way to refuse.

We can measure the success of the brain surgery in two ways; firstly by giving the model 100 harmful requests and finding the refusal rate (in my case, refusals dropped from 100/100 to 6/100 harmful requests). The second, arguably more important measure is KL divergence, essentially, is the model still useful, or did we break it? This measure deserves an article of its own as part of my core 'Build an LLM project', but to simplify, for each token, an LLM calculates the probability distribution of the next token spread across the model's entire vocabulary. We capture samples on the base model and on the abliterated model. KL divergence calculates how different the distributions are. A small value means similar next-token distributions on the examples measured. KL divergence is non-negative and unbounded; 1 is not a universal damage threshold. It must be interpreted alongside the dataset, averaging method, divergence direction and other capability evaluations.

The End Product - Scary & of no use to me!

I ran the resulting model on the DGX Spark with an AI-assisted interface. In a few demos to family and friends the result has been the same; shock and disbelief. The model’s willingness to respond to prompts it had previously refused quickly makes me squeamish about using it - I have no use for such a tool, nor do I want to make it available for anyone else, although many abliterated models are freely available.

In terms of security risk, my tests measured refusal rather than whether the model could carry out a sophisticated attack. Parameter count and a lack of refusals do not establish harmful capability, and fluent answers may still be wrong. I therefore cannot rank enterprise and societal risks from this experiment alone. Even so, seeing an interactive model readily answer requests it previously rejected felt unsettling.

Of far greater concern is the rapid progress being made by the major 'frontier-level' open-weight models. Reducing refusal in a more capable model could increase misuse risk, although this experiment does not quantify it. Given the ease with which the process can be performed, and the fact that, hardware limitations aside, open weights allow a determined user to modify model behaviour, that possibility is a serious concern.
